title: Run-Length Encode a Status Log
oneLiner: Compress a log of statuses into runs such as "ok x2", "fault x1", reading the input exactly once as a lazy sequence and changing nothing.
keyTakeaway: Run-length encoding groups adjacent equal items, which is exactly what itertools.groupby does (and why groupby on unsorted data gives several groups per key). In C#, one pass with the current value and a count does it. Accept any IEnumerable or iterable and read it once, so the function also works on streams and generators.
explanation:
Write RunLength(statuses), which turns a sequence of status strings into runs of equal adjacent statuses, each written as "status xN". ["ok", "ok", "fault", "ok"] gives ["ok x2", "fault x1", "ok x1"]: the last "ok" is a new run because something different came between. An empty input gives an empty list. Comparisons are exact: "OK" and "ok" are different statuses.

The input isn't a list: C# receives an IEnumerable<string> that's computed lazily, and Python an iterator, which can be read only once. So no indexing, no len(), and no going back. That's how real log processing works, on input that may not fit in memory. The function should be pure: build and return a new list.

In Python, itertools.groupby(statuses) yields (status, group) for each run of adjacent equal items; sum(1 for _ in group) or len(list(group)) counts it. In C#, keep the current status and its count in a foreach: when the next item differs, add the finished run to the result and start a new one, and don't forget the final run after the loop.

visualizationSteps.message: Start a run with the first status.
Different status: finish "ok x2" and start a new run.
Different again: finish "fault x1". This "ok" starts its own run, because runs are about neighbours.
The input has ended: add the final run. Forgetting this step is the classic bug.

complexity.note: One pass over the n statuses with O(1) work each; the output holds up to n runs (when no neighbours are equal). Only the current run is kept besides the output.

referenceSolutions.python:
from collections.abc import Iterable
from itertools import groupby


def run_length(statuses: Iterable[str]) -> list[str]:
    return [f"{status} x{sum(1 for _ in group)}" for status, group in groupby(statuses)]
